source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Curran_2001_InAndOutOfTheKHole.pdf, pp. 749–760 (all 12 pages). Text layer extracted with pdftotext -layout; all pages rendered at 150 dpi; Tables 1–4 and the results text on pp. 754–757 checked on the rendered pages. The text layer is born-digital and every number used below matched the page image.

claims.overstatement: None in the claim. The source itself uses causal language the claim rightly does not adopt (frequent use 'produces long-lasting impairments', abstract p. 749; similar on pp. 756 and 758), resting partly on correlations with day-0 (acute) recall rather than day-3 scores (p. 756).
claims.note: Day-3 numbers reproduce from Table 2: immediate story recall 4.56 against 9.16, category fluency 14.06 against 18.95; the comparison is people who used ketamine more than twice a month (mean 13.53 days a month) against people who used it twice a month or less (0.45), with no group free of ketamine, as the claim says. Qualifications the claim could add for this study: the frequent group also scored lower on letter fluency on both days, including the night when both groups had just taken ketamine (10.39 against 17.42; group F(1,35) = 18.5, p<0.001), which points to a difference that predates the night; it had less schooling (no degree holders against 4; GCSEs only 12 against 5), which the authors concede may have contributed (pp. 757–758); 15 participants reported cannabis and 12 alcohol on day 3 (p. 753). The frequent group's mean use (13.5 days a month, about 3 times a week) lies between the claim's 'frequent' (more than four times a week) and 'less often' groups of the larger study.

claims.overstatement: None. The claim reports this study's null result accurately; it compares two groups who both used ketamine, on state ratings taken 3 days after use, so it bears only indirectly on everyday-life dissociation or beliefs.
claims.note: Numbers reproduce from Table 3 (day 3 dissociation 4.56 against 3.47, schizotypal 25.28 against 28.95); recomputed t-tests p = 0.58 and 0.59. The authors expected the frequent group to score higher and offer a U-shaped relation or sample differences (nightclubs against squat parties; university education 75% against 28%) as possible reasons for the difference from Curran & Morgan (2000) (p. 758); the 28% does not reproduce from the qualifications on p. 753 (4 degree holders of 37 = 11%; with the 5 students, 24%). The single visual-analogue 'depression' rating was 20.39 against 10.21 on day 3 (Table 4) with no test reported (recomputed p = 0.12); the text's 'except for depression' (p. 755) is ambiguous. As in the 2000 paper, both scales are described as rated 1 to 5 but have totals below the number of items, implying 0–4 scoring.

anchors.extracted: Schizotypal symptomatology: day effect F(1,35) = 48.2, p<0.001, no significant group differences; dissociation: only a day effect F(1,35) = 78.1, p<0.001; both groups very high on day 0 against day 3.

Frequent (n = 18) against infrequent (n = 19), day 0 then day 3, means (SD): dissociation total 34.83 (21.60) against 39.26 (25.32), then 4.56 (6.35) against 3.47 (5.56); schizotypal total 54.11 (30.22) against 53.58 (28.39), then 25.28 (19.80) against 28.95 (21.37).

anchors.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (Our results did not confirm ...)
anchors.extracted: Hypothesis of more residual schizotypal and dissociative symptoms in the frequent group not confirmed; the 2000 ketamine group used about 3.1 times a month against 0.45 (infrequent) and 13.5 (frequent) here; the authors suggest a U-shaped relation or sample differences and urge caution given the sample sizes.

claims.overstatement: 'Both groups scored similarly low on the night' overstates the similarity: on letter fluency the more frequent group scored much lower on the night (10.39 against 17.42; group effect p<0.001, no interaction) and stayed lower on day 3; sentence judging showed a trend in the same direction (33.11 against 40.84; group p = 0.086).
claims.note: Everything else taken from this study reproduces: recruitment from clubs and squat parties within 30 minutes of reported ketamine use (p. 751); 18 using more than twice a month (13.53 days a month) against 19 using less (0.45) (Table 1); day-0 immediate recall 4.67 and 5.00, dissociation 34.83 and 39.26; more sedated and more anxious on day 0 than day 3 (p. 755); day-3 dissociation 4.56 and 3.47 and schizotypal 25.28 and 28.95 with no group differences; day-3 immediate recall 4.56 against 9.16 and delayed 4.39 against 8.05 (interactions F(1,35) = 13.5 and 6.7); category 14.06 against 18.95; frequent group's day-3 recall no better than on the night (4.67 to 4.56); 'about twice' (9.16/4.56 = 2.01; the authors say virtually double, p. 756); less schooling (p. 753). Qualifications: 15 participants reported cannabis and 12 alcohol on day 3 (p. 753); on day 3 the frequent group also rated more impaired concentration (33.11 against 12.74; interaction F(1,35) = 5.79, p<0.025) and memory (35.94 against 15.42; group F(1,35) = 5.79, p<0.025, the same statistic printed twice) (p. 755, Table 4); the frequent group rated more sedation on both days (group F(1,35) = 4.63, p<0.04). Drug-use history was recorded on day 3 (p. 752), so testers may not have known the frequency group on day 0; no blinding statement. No objective confirmation of drugs or amounts (p. 759). Added at step 2 (found while checking the card, not from its anchors): 'no better than on the night' holds for immediate recall (4.67 to 4.56); the frequent group's delayed recall rose from 3.11 to 4.39 (Table 2, p. 754).

anchors.extracted: Recruited from clubs and squat parties by snowball sampling; 37 completers, 18 people using ketamine more than twice a month and 19 using it twice a month or less; all used several drugs and had taken ketamine that evening within 30 minutes before taking part; tested on the night (day 0) and 3 days later (day 3) with balanced test versions; day-3 session usually at home (p. 752).

Typical use 13.53 (6.18) against 0.45 (0.80) days a month, t(35) = 8.92. key_findings.correction: The note's last sentence holds for immediate recall only: the frequent group's immediate recall was 4.67 on day 0 and 4.56 on day 3, but its delayed recall rose from 3.11 to 4.39 (Table 2, p. 754; Figure 1, p. 755). Suggested wording: the frequent group's day-3 immediate recall was no higher than its recall while intoxicated on day 0; its delayed recall rose from 3.11 to 4.39. The rest of the finding, and F(1,35) = 6.7 giving p = 0.014, reproduce.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high overall for the causal reading. Outcome measurement at some concerns rather than high is defensible here, since drug-use history was recorded on day 3 (p. 752), so testers may not have known the frequency group on day 0.

interpretation_gap.note: Severe, given the abstract's causal and public-health conclusions (p. 749). One detail to correct: results_show says the frequent group's recall was no better than on the night; that holds for immediate recall only (delayed rose from 3.11 to 4.39), as for key finding 5.

missed: The authors argue that ketamine's short elimination half-life rules out residual effects of the night's dose by day 3 (pp. 750, 758), without considering metabolites, after-effects or withdrawal in people using about every other day (13.5 days a month; five at 20 to 24 days, p. 758). The frequent group's higher self-rated sedation on both days, impaired concentration and memory on day 3, and nausea (p. 755) fit after-effects or withdrawal as well as chronic effects; the interpretation gap does not take up this argument.

The authors attribute the groups' similar day-0 performance, despite larger self-reported day-0 amounts in the frequent group, to tolerance (p. 758); relevant to any claim that the two groups were similarly affected on the night.
